{{Short description|Class of algorithms in information theory}}
The term '''Blahut–Arimoto algorithm''' is often used to refer to a class of [[algorithm]]s for computing numerically either the [[Information theory|information theoretic]] [[Channel capacity|capacity]] of a channel, the [[Rate-distortion theory|rate-distortion]] function of a source or a source encoding (i.e. compression to remove the redundancy). They are [[Iterative method|iterative algorithms]] that eventually converge to one of the maxima of the [[optimization problem]] that is associated with these information theoretic concepts.

==History and application==
For the case of [[channel capacity]], the algorithm was independently invented by [[Suguru Arimoto]]<ref>{{citation | first = Suguru | last = Arimoto | s2cid = 8408706 | author-link = Suguru Arimoto | title = An algorithm for computing the capacity of arbitrary discrete memoryless channels | journal = [[IEEE Transactions on Information Theory]] | volume = 18 | issue = 1 | pages=14–20 | year = 1972 | doi = 10.1109/TIT.1972.1054753 }}.</ref> and [[Richard Blahut]].<ref>{{citation | first = Richard | last = Blahut | author-link = Richard Blahut | title = Computation of channel capacity and rate-distortion functions | journal = [[IEEE Transactions on Information Theory]] | volume = 18 | issue = 4 | pages=460–473 | year = 1972 | doi = 10.1109/TIT.1972.1054855 | citeseerx = 10.1.1.133.7174 }}.</ref> In addition, Blahut's treatment gives algorithms for computing [[rate–distortion theory|rate distortion]] and generalized [[channel capacity|capacity]] with input contraints (i.e. the capacity-cost function, analogous to rate-distortion). These algorithms are most applicable to the case of arbitrary finite alphabet sources. Much work has been done to extend it to more general problem instances.<ref>{{cite conference |title=A Generalized Blahut–Arimoto Algorithm |first=Pascal O. |last=Vontobel |book-title=Proceedings IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory, 2003 |date=2003 |page=53 |doi=10.1109/ISIT.2003.1228067 |isbn=0-7803-7728-1 |url=https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?repid=rep1&type=pdf&doi=9fb198aba311eda67b3c53c6f60db2b06c011ad4}}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv
 | eprint = 1012.5071v2
 | author1 = Iddo Naiss
 | author2 = Haim Permuter|author2-link=Haim Permuter
 | title = Extension of the Blahut-Arimoto algorithm for maximizing directed information
 | class = cs.IT
 | year = 2010}}</ref>
Recently, a version of the algorithm that accounts for continuous and multivariate outputs was proposed with applications in cellular signaling.<ref>{{citation| journal = [[PLOS Computational Biology]]|volume = 15|issue = 7|article-number = e1007132|doi = 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1007132|pmid = 31299056|pmc = 6655862|title=Information-theoretic analysis of multivariate single-cell signaling responses|author1= Tomasz Jetka|author2= Karol Nienaltowski|author3= Tomasz Winarski| author4=Slawomir Blonski| author5= Michal Komorowski|year=2019|bibcode = 2019PLSCB..15E7132J|arxiv = 1808.05581 | doi-access=free }}</ref> There exists also a version of Blahut–Arimoto algorithm for [[directed information]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Naiss |first1=Iddo |last2=Permuter |first2=Haim H. |title=Extension of the Blahut–Arimoto Algorithm for Maximizing Directed Information |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |date=January 2013 |volume=59 |issue=1 |pages=204–222 |doi=10.1109/TIT.2012.2214202|arxiv=1012.5071 |bibcode=2013ITIT...59..204N |s2cid=3115749 }}</ref>

== Algorithm for Channel Capacity ==
A discrete memoryless channel (DMC) can be specified using two random variables <math>X, Y
</math> with alphabet <math>\mathcal X, \mathcal Y</math>, and a channel law as a [[conditional probability distribution]] <math>p(y|x)</math>. The [[channel capacity]], defined as <math>C := \sup_{p \sim X}I(X;Y)</math>, indicates the maximum efficiency that a channel can communicate, in the unit of bit per use.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cover |first=T. M. |title=Elements of information theory |date=2006 |publisher=Wiley-Interscience |others=Joy A. Thomas |isbn=0-471-24195-4 |edition=2nd |location=Hoboken, N.J. |oclc=59879802}}</ref> Now if we denote the cardinality <math>|\mathcal X| = n, |\mathcal Y| = m</math>, then <math>p_{Y|X}</math> is a <math>n \times m</math> matrix, which we denote the <math>i^{th}</math> row, <math>j^{th}</math> column entry by <math>w_{ij}</math>. For the case of [[channel capacity]], the algorithm was independently invented by [[Suguru Arimoto]]<ref name=":0">{{citation | first = Suguru | last = Arimoto | s2cid = 8408706 | author-link = Suguru Arimoto | title = An algorithm for computing the capacity of arbitrary discrete memoryless channels | journal = [[IEEE Transactions on Information Theory]] | volume = 18 | issue = 1 | pages=14–20 | year = 1972 | doi = 10.1109/TIT.1972.1054753 }}.</ref> and [[Richard Blahut]].<ref name=":1">{{citation | first = Richard | last = Blahut | author-link = Richard Blahut | title = Computation of channel capacity and rate-distortion functions | journal = [[IEEE Transactions on Information Theory]] | volume = 18 | issue = 4 | pages=460–473 | year = 1972 | doi = 10.1109/TIT.1972.1054855 | citeseerx = 10.1.1.133.7174 }}.</ref> They both found the following expression for the capacity of a DMC with channel law: 

<math>C = \max_{\mathbf p} \max_{Q} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m  p _i w_{ij}\log\left(\dfrac {Q_{ji}}{p_i}\right)</math> 

where <math>\mathbf p</math> and <math>Q</math> are maximized over the following requirements: 

* <math>\mathbf p</math> is a probability distribution on <math>X</math>, That is, if we write <math>\mathbf p </math> as  <math>(p_1, p_2 ... , p_n), \sum_{i= 1}^np_i = 1</math>
* <math>Q = (q_{ji})</math> is a <math>m \times n</math> matrix that behaves like a transition matrix from <math>Y</math> to <math>X</math> with respect to the channel law. That is, For all <math>1 \leq i \leq n, 1\leq j \leq m</math>:
** <math>q_{ji} \geq 0, q_{ji} = 0 \Leftrightarrow w_{ij} = 0</math>
** Every row sums up to 1, i.e. <math>\sum_{i=1}^n q_{ji} = 1</math>.

Then upon picking a random probability distribution <math>\mathbf p^0 := (p^0_1, p^0_2, ... p^0_n)</math> on <math>X</math>, we can generate a sequence <math>(\mathbf p^0, Q^0, \mathbf p^1, Q^1 ...)</math> iteratively as follows:

<math>(q^t_{ji}):= \dfrac{p^t_iw_{ij}}{\sum_{k=1}^n p^t_kw_{kj}}</math>

<math>p^{t+1}_k := \dfrac {\prod_{j = 1}^m (q^t_{jk})^{w_{kj}}}{\sum_{i= 1}^n\prod_{j = 1}^m(q^t_{ji})^{w_{ij}}}
</math>

For <math>t = 0, 1, 2 ...</math>.

Then, using the theory of optimization, specifically [[coordinate descent]], Yeung<ref>{{Cite book |last=Yeung |first=Raymond W. |title=Information theory and network coding |date=2008 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-0-387-79234-7 |location=New York |oclc=288469056}}</ref> showed that the sequence indeed converges to the required maximum. That is, 

<math>\lim_{t\to \infty}  \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m  p^t_i w_{ij}\log\left(\dfrac {Q^t_{ji}}{p^t_i}\right) = C</math>.

So given a channel law <math>p(y|x)</math>, the capacity can be numerically estimated up to arbitrary precision.

==Algorithm for Rate-Distortion==
Suppose we have a source <math>X</math> with probability <math>p(x)</math> of any given symbol.  We wish to find an encoding <math>p(\hat{x}|x)</math> that generates a [[Lossy compression|compressed]] signal <math>\hat{X}</math> from the original signal while minimizing the expected [[distortion]] <math>\langle d(x,\hat{x}) \rangle</math>, where the expectation is taken over the joint probability of <math>X</math> and <math>\hat{X}</math>.  We can find an encoding that minimizes the rate-distortion functional locally by repeating the following iteration until convergence:

:<math>p_{t+1}(\hat{x}|x) = \frac{p_t(\hat{x}) \exp(-\beta d(x,\hat{x}))}{\sum_{\hat{x}} p_t(\hat{x}) \exp(-\beta d(x,\hat{x}))}</math>

:<math>p_{t+1}(\hat{x}) = \sum_{x} p(x)p_{t+1}(\hat{x}|x)</math>

where <math>\beta</math> is a parameter related to the slope in the rate-distortion curve that we are targeting and thus is related to how much we favor compression versus distortion (higher <math>\beta</math> means less compression).
